I read the test and the target function. The test constructs four `InlineQueryResultArticle` objects in `results` and calls `bot._effective_inline_results(results=results, next_offset="next_77")`.

In `_effective_inline_results`, the method first gets `effective_results` from `super()._effective_inline_results(...)`. Then, because the bot in the test is created with `arbitrary_callback_data=True`, the callback data cache is intended to be active, so the code does not take the early return at line 691-692. Instead it initializes `results = []` and loops over each item in `effective_results`.

Inside that loop, every item here is an `InlineQueryResultArticle` with a `reply_markup`, so the `else` branch runs each time. At line 702, `new_result = copy(result)` makes a shallow copy of the current `result` before any markup replacement happens. Therefore, the values assigned to `new_result` are just the copied per-item `InlineQueryResultArticle` objects as they appear in `effective_results` at loop entry.

From the test setup, those four articles are:
1. `art_1` with title `Title 1`, description `desc 1`, payload `payload 1`, and `keyboard_a`
2. `art_2` with title `Title 2`, description `desc 2`, payload `payload 2`, and `keyboard_b`
3. `art_3` with title `Title 3`, description `desc 3`, payload `payload 3`, and `keyboard_c`
4. `art_4` with title `Title 4`, description `desc 4`, payload `payload 4`, and again `keyboard_a`

Because the assignment happens before lines 703-705 mutate `new_result.reply_markup`, the sequence we need is the pre-mutation copied objects, preserving the original structured callback data dictionaries in their markups.
